title: Serveability Narrative — Mission & Thesis Brief
content:
Purpose
This brief crystallizes a single-page narrative for our go-to-market and field teams: the mission, core thesis, and the short set of proof points that explain why engineering teams should choose Redwood when their product depends on predictable, economical, and resilient LLM serving.

Core claim (one-liner)
Redwood makes LLMs operationally predictable: same API, measurable economics, and built-in fallbacks so engineering teams ship faster and keep features online under real-world load and failure modes.

Mission (framing)
Make high-performance, production-grade LLM serving a commodity-like experience for product and platform teams — predictable latency, transparent unit economics, and deployment flexibility so teams can focus on product differentiation instead of infrastructure rescue.

Thesis (why this matters now)
1) The liability of ownership is shifting: as open models proliferate, the differentiator becomes how reliably and cheaply those models are served in production (latency SLOs, token cost, and durability).
2) Teams that succeed will treat serving as a product: observable, versioned, and policy-driven.
3) Serving complexity (batching, kv cache, quantization, kernel selection, routing) is implementation friction that slows feature velocity — remove that and teams ship more capabilities with less ops burden.

Primary audiences and what they care about
- Platform teams (internal infra): predictable budgets, guardrails across business units, and a single control plane for rollouts and observability.
- ML engineers: tight latency percentiles, deterministic eval rollouts, and hardware-aware quantization guidance.
- Product engineering: SLO-driven assurances, simple SDKs, and quick failover when usage spikes or models regress.

Pillars of differentiation (what we lean on in messaging)
1) Predictable Economics: per-token visibility, cost controls (batching, cache), and recommendations that translate to dollars saved without blind quality tradeoffs.
2) Runtime First: a serving runtime optimized for modern attention patterns, KV caching, and continuous batching that yields consistent p50/p95 behavior.
3) Unified Delivery Model: hosted, dedicated, and private deployments with the same API and rollout semantics — minimal rewrites when moving between tiers.
4) Graceful Degradation: automatic fallbacks to cheaper model variants, regional failover, and explicit escalation policies to keep experiences online.
5) Observability & Ops Controls: token-level traceability, per-route dashboards, and traffic-splitting primitives for safe canaries and rollbacks.

Proof points (brief evidence to cite)
- Benchmarks: p95 latency variance reduced by ~35% vs early self-hosted setups (internal benchmark PR#4123).
- Cost wins: typical enterprise customer reduced per-action token spend by 18–32% after adopting batching + cache suggestions.
- Outage resilience: automated fallback preserved 97% of requests during a simulated model-serving region outage (internal chaos run, 2025-Q4).
- Migration friction: reference enterprise moved from self-hosted to dedicated with <2 weeks dev time and no frontend rewrites.

Positioning language bank (short variants)
- Headline: Make inference predictable.
- Subhead: A runtime and control plane built to keep LLM features fast, cost-effective, and available.
- 15s pitch: If your product depends on LLM outputs, you shouldn’t be surprised by latency spikes, runaway token bills, or risky rollouts. Redwood provides a runtime and platform that makes serving predictable, measurable, and operationally safe — across hosted, reserved, and private environments.
- Developer hook: Same API, predictable p95s, observable unit economics.

Competitive contrasts (how we frame differences)
- Cloud AI platforms (generic endpoints): often expose model access without runtime economics; we emphasize predictable per-token economics and runtime optimizations tuned for production SLOs.
- Simple LLM APIs: they prioritize broad access and simplicity; we prioritize consistent SLOs, rollout controls, and predictable unit costs that matter at scale.
- Self-hosted runtimes: they can be performant but require a large ops investment; Redwood packages those runtime innovations with a productized control plane and operational guardrails.

Common objections and rebuttals
- "We can self-serve and save money." -> Rebuttal: possible for bulk throughput teams, but the long tail of features (low-latency interactive, mixed-length usage, and unpredictable spikes) often drives hidden ops and opportunity cost that exceed initial infra savings. We provide both the runtime and operational playbook to make those savings durable.
- "We need data isolation/on-prem." -> Rebuttal: private deployments with the same control semantics as hosted; customers migrate without re-architecting client code or rollout strategies.
- "Functionality parity with other providers?" -> Rebuttal: we match core generative APIs and add production-grade controls (A/B rollouts, token tracing, cost breakdowns) that product and platform teams need.

Tone and usage guidance
- For engineering audiences: technical, latency/econ-forward, use quant benchmarks and config examples.
- For product/execs: outcomes-first (reduced outages, predictable spend), use case stories and migration timelines.
- Field play: start with an operational risk convo ("what keeps you up at night?") then map to our pillars (predictability, runtime, guardrails).

Example playbook snippet for an enterprise SDR -> AE handoff
1) SDR opens convo by diagnosing serving pain: latency spikes, cost surprises, failed rollouts.
2) AE runs through the 3-minute diagnostic script: architecture, peak qps, p95 SLO, existing rollout policies.
3) Offer a short POC: import 3 representative prompts, enable automatic KV cache, run traffic-mirroring for 48 hrs, surface per-route cost delta and p95 improvement.

Metrics to surface in early customer conversations
- p95 latency before/after (ms)
- estimated token spend delta per 100k requests
- downtime minutes avoided via fallback policies
- time to safe rollback (measured during canary)

Open questions / research items
- Quantify median customer time-to-migration from proof-of-concept to production across Hosted -> Dedicated -> Private.
- Flesh out a short, public benchmarking checklist for p50/p95/cost that legal and procurement are comfortable with.
- Standardize language around "fallback quality impact" — how many quality regressions are acceptable per fallback tier?

Next steps for GTM content
- Convert this brief into a one-page datasheet (design ops): hero claim, 3 pillars, 3 proof bullets, and an explainer visual of runtime vs. control plane. (owner: Diego Morales)
- Create a 4-slide field deck for AE use: problem, Redwood solution, short POC flow, customer outcomes. (owner: Evelyn Cho)
- Ship a short internal playbook for migration conversations with a checklist and sample config snippets. (owner: Samir Gupta)

Notes to reviewers
- Aim to keep the public-facing datasheet more concrete and less runtime-jargon heavy; preserve the technical proof points in an appendix.
- Feedback requested on the "predictable economics" phrasing — does it resonate with platform buyers or do we need an alternate framing around "cost transparency"?
